items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern is counseling a patient about a new inhaler. The intern's supervising pharmacist leaves for an off-site appointment during the conversation. Another pharmacist is on the premises but has not been told about the intern's task. The first pharmacist can be reached by telephone. What should happen before the consultation and dispensing are completed?

choices.text: Continue under the departed pharmacist's telephone oversight; ask the on-site pharmacist to check the prescription afterward.
choices.why: Incorrect. A preceptor's availability by telephone from off-site does not meet the Board policy's on-premises direct-supervision conditions.

choices.text: Let the intern finish both counseling and final validation because direct supervision was present when the interaction began.
choices.why: Incorrect. Supervision cannot be presumed to continue after the responsible pharmacist leaves, and an intern does not independently perform the licensed pharmacist's final validation.

choices.text: Have the on-site pharmacist take over direct supervision, actively supervise counseling, and complete final validation.
choices.why: Correct. A different pharmacist may take over direct supervision when the preceptor is unavailable; the consultation requires active supervision and a licensed pharmacist performs final validation.

choices.text: Have the certified technician finish the drug-use discussion while the second pharmacist records the intern's earlier work.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technicians can make an appropriately trained offer to counsel but may not perform the clinical patient counseling.

source_evidence.finding: If preceptor unavailable another pharmacist must directly supervise; preceptor on premises, fully aware, readily available; actively present for consultation.
Intern direct-supervision and counseling role; final dispensing validation belongs to licensed pharmacist.

items.note: New decisive fact: the preceptor leaves midway and replacement pharmacist has not assumed the supervision role. Distinct from E30-003 and E30-076.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is providing vaccination services. One pharmacist would supervise SIX Massachusetts-licensed support personnel, all actively preparing or filling prescriptions. All applicable intern-supervision and training requirements are satisfied; there is no waiver or dedicated trainer. Which roster qualifies for the Board's vaccination-service 1:6 ratio?

choices.text: One certified technician, one pharmacy intern, and four noncertified technicians.
choices.why: Incorrect. Only two people in this roster meet the specified certified-technician/intern composition requirement.

choices.text: Three pharmacy interns and three noncertified technicians, with no certified technician.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy permits counting up to two interns toward the three qualifying personnel, and specifies certified technicians as part of the qualifying composition.

choices.text: Two certified technicians and four noncertified technicians, without an intern.
choices.why: Incorrect. Although all six are licensed, only two of them are certified technicians; the 1:6 exception requires at least three qualifying personnel.

choices.text: One certified technician, two pharmacy interns, and three noncertified technicians.
choices.why: Correct. Three qualifying personnel include one licensed certified technician and two licensed pharmacy interns; this fits the maximum of six.

source_evidence.finding: Vaccination-service pharmacies: maximum 1:6; at least three qualifying licensed certified technicians, counting up to two licensed pharmacy interns.
Intern supervision and context limitations remain applicable.

items.note: Roster-based 1:6 exception differs from the ordinary 1:4 team in E30-026.

items.stem: A Massachusetts clinic issues a new Schedule IV prescription using electronic prescribing of controlled substances (EPCS). The prescriber is properly authorized, and the drug, patient, and clinical details are otherwise valid. Which workflow produces a properly signed and transmitted ELECTRONIC controlled-substance prescription? Assume no qualifying transmission failover.

choices.text: An assistant drafts it; the prescriber gives verbal approval; the assistant uses the prescriber's shared token and password to sign and transmit.
choices.why: Incorrect. The named practitioner must personally complete the two-factor signing protocol and may not share their credential with office staff.

choices.text: An assistant drafts it; the named prescriber reviews and signs with their own two-factor credential; the unchanged order is sent electronically.
choices.why: Correct. An agent may enter draft data, but the named prescribing practitioner reviews and signs using their own credential; the signed record may then be transmitted without alteration.

choices.text: The prescriber signs it electronically; staff then change the ordered quantity without another signature and transmit the modified prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Altering DEA-required prescription information after electronic signing cancels that signed prescription; the changed record cannot simply be sent under the old signature.

choices.text: The prescriber signs it in the EPCS application; the office then prints and faxes a copy as the electronic transmission without a verified failover.
choices.why: Incorrect. A printed-and-faxed copy is not an electronically transmitted EPCS order; Massachusetts excludes unverified ordinary-fax conversions from valid electronic transmission.

source_evidence.finding: Agent draft allowed; named practitioner signs with own two-factor credential; signed DEA content cannot be altered/transmitted as though unchanged; printing is not electronic transmission.

source_evidence.section: DEA Diversion Control EPCS FAQ, agent drafting and practitioner signing
source_evidence.finding: Staff may prepare draft but prescribing practitioner reviews, approves, signs via two-factor protocol.
Electronic prescription transmitted by means other than electronic transmission is invalid absent verified failover.

items.note: Avoid confusion between authorized drafting and unauthorized use of practitioner signing credentials; a different legal decision from E30-123.

items.topic: Offer, later refusal and counseling record
items.stem: At a Massachusetts community pharmacy, a properly trained technician offers pharmacist counseling for a new oral prescription. The patient initially accepts, then says 'I have changed my mind; I decline counseling' before speaking with a pharmacist or intern. A printed drug leaflet is in the bag. The staff record says 'Counseling completed.' Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The printed leaflet satisfies the actual clinical counseling requirement because a new drug therapy is involved.
choices.why: Incorrect. Written material does not turn an offer or a declined conversation into clinical counseling by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern.

choices.text: The trained technician may have made a valid offer even though the technician did not personally provide clinical counseling.
choices.why: Correct. Under 247 CMR 9.18(1)–(3), a properly trained designee may offer the pharmacist's counseling services; only pharmacists and pharmacy interns may perform counseling.

choices.text: The initial acceptance means the pharmacy must record counseling as completed even if the patient leaves without a consultation.
choices.why: Incorrect. An initial yes is not evidence that counseling occurred; the later refusal changes the encounter and should be captured accurately.

choices.text: The later refusal should be recorded accurately, and the completed-counseling entry should not be used to describe this encounter.
choices.why: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §21A does not force counseling when the patient declines and directs reasonable efforts to record a failure to accept counseling.

source_evidence.finding: Offer, acceptance, counseling, later refusal, and reasonable effort to record failure to accept; absent refusal record presumption noted.
Trained designee may offer; clinical counseling is performed by pharmacist or intern.

items.note: The patient changes their choice before counseling; do not infer a completed conversation from acceptance or leaflet.

items.topic: Emergency oral Schedule II partial-fill clock
items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives an authorized emergency ORAL Schedule II prescription at 9:00 a.m. Monday for 30 tablets, an appropriate emergency-period quantity. Although all 30 are available, the patient requests only 10 at 6:00 p.m. Monday, and the pharmacist properly records a patient-requested partial fill. All other emergency-prescription and record requirements are satisfied. At 10:00 a.m. Thursday, the SAME pharmacy receives the patient's request for the remaining 20 tablets. What should the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Require a new prescription: the emergency oral partial-fill deadline passed 72 hours after the order was issued Monday morning.
choices.why: Correct. Under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2), the remaining part of an emergency oral Schedule II prescription requested as a partial fill must be dispensed no later than 72 hours after issuance; 73 hours have elapsed.

choices.text: Dispense the balance because the 72-hour clock began with the first partial dispensing at 6:00 p.m. Monday.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 72-hour window measured from the first partial fill applies to the stock-shortage pathway, not a patient-requested partial fill of an emergency oral prescription.

choices.text: Dispense the balance because every patient-requested Schedule II partial fill remains fillable for 30 days after issuance.
choices.why: Incorrect. The ordinary 30-day patient-requested rule contains a specific 72-hour-from-issuance limit for emergency oral prescriptions.

choices.text: Use the emergency follow-up documentation to restart the remaining-quantity window when the paper prescription reaches the pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Delivery of a compliant emergency follow-up prescription does not restart the separate request-based partial-fill deadline.

source_evidence.finding: For patient/prescriber requested partial fill of emergency oral Schedule II, balance no later than 72 hours after the prescription is ISSUED.
Stock-shortage pathway: 72 hours from initial partial fill, separately identified from request-based pathway.
MA patient-requested partial dispensing at same pharmacy subject to federal law; emergency oral issuance constraints and follow-up obligations.

items.note: Monday 09:00 → Thursday 10:00 = 73 hours since ISSUE; Monday 18:00 → Thursday 10:00 = 64 hours since first partial dispensing. Do not confuse the clocks.

items.topic: Prescriber PPPA packaging instruction after transfer
items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a lawful transfer of the remaining refills of a prescription for an oral medicine subject to federal child-resistant packaging requirements. The original prescriber specifically directed CONVENTIONAL (non-child-resistant) packaging for THAT prescription, and the instruction is included in the accurate transfer record. No separate patient blanket request or product exemption exists. What is the BEST packaging choice for the next refill?

choices.text: Use child-resistant packaging because a prescriber's specific packaging instruction expires when a refill is transferred.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal packaging exception can apply to refills of the same prescription; transferring the remaining refills does not itself convert the order into a different prescription.

choices.text: Use conventional packaging for all later prescriptions written for this patient, even without a general patient request.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prescriber instruction tied to one prescription is not a blanket patient waiver covering other prescriptions.

choices.text: Honor the documented prescriber's direction for the remaining refill of this same prescription.
choices.why: Correct. CPSC guidance permits a prescriber-specific conventional packaging instruction to carry to refills of that prescription; the pharmacy must confirm the order's scope.

choices.text: Ask the patient to issue a new waiver because a prescriber's packaging direction has no effect beyond the first dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prescriber can order conventional packaging for the prescription, including its refills; a new patient request is not necessarily required for the same prescription.

items.citation: 15 U.S.C. §1473(b); 16 CFR 1701.1(b),(d); CPSC PPPA Healthcare Professional Guide (January 2023), FAQ p.12

source_evidence.section: CPSC 2023 PPPA Guide, p. 12, prescriber standing request
source_evidence.finding: Specific prescriber conventional-packaging instructions can be followed for refills of the same prescription, not other prescriptions.
Dispensing pharmacist responsible for special packaging unless prescriber order or consumer request supports conventional packaging.

items.note: The original prescriber's instruction covers this prescription's refills, not an unrelated prescription; no unsupported documentation mandate is claimed.

items.topic: Media-fill pass with failed post-test gloved-fingertip sampling
items.stem: At a Massachusetts Category 2 sterile-compounding pharmacy, a technician passes a media-fill simulation but the gloved fingertip/thumb sampling collected immediately afterward exceeds the applicable action level. The supervisor suggests closing the assessment as a pass because the media-fill container showed no growth. Under the official USP <797> interpretation, what is the BEST response?

choices.text: Close the assessment as passed because the media-fill culture is a more direct sterility test than the glove sample.
choices.why: Incorrect. Passing the media fill does not cancel a separate failed post-media-fill gloved-fingertip/thumb component.

choices.text: Repeat only the media fill next week and disregard the glove finding once the new simulated preparation shows no growth.
choices.why: Incorrect. Repeating an unrelated passing component does not resolve the failed gloved-fingertip sampling or required investigation.

choices.text: Assume USP mandates automatic shutdown of all compounding across the facility until every worker completes three entirely new media fills.
choices.why: Incorrect. USP FAQ Q53 states that the chapter does not itself impose universal automatic cessation; the facility must evaluate the failure, take and document appropriate corrective action.

choices.text: Record an overall competency failure, investigate the cause, and document corrective actions and appropriate reassessment.
choices.why: Correct. The post-media-fill fingertip component is independently required; a failure makes the aseptic manipulation competency fail, and corrective-action investigation and records are required.

items.citation: USP <797> §§2.2–2.3 and 20; USP official FAQ (Dec 11, 2023), Q53; WA DOH 2026 USP <797> self-inspection addendum, §2.3 quoted text

source_evidence.finding: No across-the-board automatic cessation under USP chapter; evaluate cause, determine corrective actions, document.

source_evidence.section: WA Department of Health January 2026 addendum, §2.3 quoted requirement, p.8, questions 17–18
source_evidence.finding: Failed media-fill, post-media-fill gloved-fingertip or surface sampling component constitutes overall aseptic-competency failure; results and corrective action documented.
MA pharmacy compounding compliance with applicable USP standards.

items.note: SOURCE CAVEAT: USP FAQ and 2026 state regulatory addendum give the exact needed proposition, but subscription USP–NF chapter original was not directly retrieved. Independent reviewer must determine whether this is sufficient for a legally approved final item; HOLD until then.

items.topic: Orange Book AB1 versus AB2 comparison
items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a prescription for **Brand R**, a hypothetical extended-release Drug M tablet, 10 mg. The patient and prescriber allow lawful interchange. A supplied FDA-style therapeutic-equivalence table shows: Brand R = AB1; Generic P = AB1; Generic Q = AB2; Generic S = BX. Each generic has the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route; each is less expensive and reasonably available. Assume no other Massachusetts exception or clinical concern. Which generic is FDA-rated therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed product?

choices.text: Generic P, because its AB1 code matches the exact equivalence group assigned to Brand R.
choices.why: Correct. FDA says products with three-character codes are therapeutically equivalent only to products with that same AB-number code.

choices.text: Generic Q, because every AB-number code is therapeutically equivalent to every other AB-number code.
choices.why: Incorrect. AB1 and AB2 represent distinct equivalence groups in the FDA Orange Book; identical ingredients and strengths do not remove the distinction.

choices.text: Generic S, because BX denotes an approved drug whose bioequivalence problems have all been resolved.
choices.why: Incorrect. BX is a B-category designation rather than an A-rated therapeutically equivalent comparison for the prescribed reference group.

choices.text: Generic Q or Generic S, because either same-strength extended-release product qualifies without regard to its FDA code.
choices.why: Incorrect. Same ingredient, route, dosage form and strength alone do not establish therapeutic equivalence when the FDA assigns different or B-category codes.

items.citation: FDA Orange Book Preface §1.7 (AB/AB1/AB2), 105 CMR 720.050(a), 720.200 Appendix A; M.G.L. c.112 §12D

source_evidence.section: FDA Orange Book Preface §1.7, AB1/AB2 codes
source_evidence.finding: Within the same heading only exact same three-character AB code indicates therapeutic equivalence; AB1 not interchangeable with AB2.
When no 'no substitution', state interchange mandate/availability rules and exceptions apply.
MA automatic adoption of FDA A-rated interchangeable products, with state conditions.

items.note: All names are hypothetical table values, not actual Orange Book product entries. This is a code-interpretation task, not a claim that Drug M is a real product.
